source: Dayan (1993) Improving generalisation for temporal difference learning: the successor representation
finding: Defines the successor representation (SR). Each state is described by the discounted expected number of future visits to every other state. TD learning can learn the SR itself. With a linear value function, value = SR times expected immediate reward, so the temporal part of the task is factored out.
numbers: Formula: M = (I - gamma P)^-1. Learned with the TD rule, using successor prediction errors. Demo: grid maze with a barrier, comparing a punctate code, CMAC squares and the SR.
limits: The SR is tied to the policy that generated it. Small toy task, no human data.
agent_relevance: Memory design: store for each class of situation 'where does this lead' as a table of expected successors, then combine with a separate, cheap reward vector. A reward change then costs one edit, not a re-plan.
quote: Appropriate generalisation between states is determined by how similar their successors are

source: Dayan (1993) Improving generalisation for temporal difference learning: the successor representation (latent learning result)
finding: In the grid navigation task, an SR learned in an unrewarded exploration phase (latent learning) speeds later reward learning. The learned SR respects the barrier: states on opposite sides share few predictions even if close in space.
numbers: Figures 3-4 give learning curves only (SR with and without latent learning vs punctate and CMAC codes). No sample size or p-values: single simulations.
limits: The paper says the learned SR could hinder learning if the goal moves to a place the old policy rarely visited. Policy dependence is the core weakness.
agent_relevance: Exploration before the goal is known gives reusable structure, but structure cached under one policy can mislead after the goal changes. Tag cached structure with the goal or plan class that produced it.

source: Daw, Niv, Dayan (2005) Uncertainty-based competition between prefrontal and dorsolateral striatal systems for behavioral control
finding: Proposed that model-based (tree search, prefrontal) and model-free (cached, dorsolateral striatal) controllers each track their own uncertainty, and the more certain one controls the action. Not opened: fetch returned only HTML shell.
numbers: none recorded (not opened)
limits: Arbitration by uncertainty has had mixed direct tests. Described from memory only.
agent_relevance: Arbitration rule: use the cheap cached route when its uncertainty is low, simulate when it is high. A signal-based trigger, in line with G1.

source: Daw, Gershman, Seymour, Dayan, Dolan (2011) Model-based influences on humans' choices and striatal prediction errors
finding: Introduced the two-step task. First-stage choice follows reward (a model-free sign) but also depends on whether the previous transition was common or rare (a model-based sign). Both signs are present in the same people.
numbers: N=17 adults, 201 trials in 3 blocks of 67. Reward main effect p<1e-8. Reward x transition interaction p<5e-5. No main effect of transition (p=.5). Median weight on model-free values 61%, model-based 39% (sign tests vs 0 and 100%, P<.005). Model beat chance for all 17 (p<.05). Reward effect positive for 14/17, interaction positive for 10/17.
limits: Small sample. Later work shows the stay-probability signature can arise from model-free strategies (Akam 2015) and the task gives no payoff for planning (Kool 2016).
agent_relevance: Humans mix cached and simulated values rather than choosing one. A hybrid weight is a tunable quantity for the agent.

source: Daw et al. (2011) Neuron, fMRI part
finding: The ventral striatal BOLD prediction-error signal, long taken as a pure model-free signal, also carried model-based information, in proportions matching those that best explained each person's choices.
numbers: Same N=17. Summary: signal 'reflected both model-free and model-based predictions in proportions matching those that best explained choice behavior'.
limits: Challenges a clean split of two learners; later fMRI work is mixed on how pure each system is.
agent_relevance: Do not assume cache and planner stay separate. Planner output can train the cache, and their disagreement is a usable signal.

source: Momennejad, Russek, Cheong, Botvinick, Daw, Gershman (2017) The successor representation in human reinforcement learning
finding: Design: reward revaluation versus transition revaluation. Model-based predicts equal success on both. Model-free predicts failure on both. A pure SR predicts success on reward change, failure on transition change, because the SR caches multi-step visits and cannot be edited without re-experience. Humans: strong on reward change, weaker but above zero on transition change.
numbers: Experiment 1 (passive learning, N=58 kept of 69). Revaluation score: reward 0.5199 (SE 0.0203), transition 0.4503 (SE 0.0229), control 0.0310. ANOVA F(2,1154)=38.77, P<.001. Reward vs transition t(57)=2.89, P=.016 (Bonferroni). Each vs control P<.001. Control not different from zero (P=.22).
limits: The reward vs transition gap is small (about 0.07 on a 0 to 1 scale). A pure SR predicts zero for transition, so a hybrid is needed. Exclusions were large (4 did not finish, 7 failed the attention check).
agent_relevance: People cache multi-step successor structure: fast update when what-it-is-worth changes, slow when what-leads-to-what changes. Warning for the agent: a cached 'where does this lead' memory goes stale silently when structure changes.
quote: SR-based algorithms ... predict that an agent will be insensitive to transition revaluation but sensitive to reward revaluation

source: Momennejad et al. (2017), response times and model fit
finding: Response times at test were slowest after transition revaluation, as if people fall back on effortful model-based recomputation just when the cache fails. Only a linear SR+MB hybrid captured the asymmetry.
numbers: RT main effect F(2,171)=7.74, P<.001. Transition slower than reward t(57)=2.08, P<.05; transition slower than control t(57)=4.04, P<.001; reward slower than control t(57)=3.56, P<.001.
limits: The hybrid was a simple linear mix of ratings, fitted by grid search on group means (squared error). Other hybrids (SR plus replay) are not excluded.
agent_relevance: A slow-down at the moment the cache is wrong is a cheap signal to trigger re-planning. For an LLM scaffold the analogue is a cache miss or a failed prediction check.

source: Momennejad et al. (2017) Experiment 2: sequential decision task with policy revaluation
finding: Replicated and extended Exp 1 with active choice. Added policy revaluation: a new big reward deep in the tree changes the best earlier action with no change in transitions. A pure SR cannot solve this either. People behaved like transition revaluation, not like reward revaluation.
numbers: N=88 kept of 112 recruited on Mechanical Turk (27 excluded for failing to learn the phase 1 policy). Reward vs policy contrast -0.6592, Z=-2.61, P=.0043. Policy vs transition contrast 0.14, Z=0.56, P=.5771. Reward>control contrast 3.1078 (Z=6.95); transition>control 2.31 (Z=5.11); policy>control 2.45 (Z=5.20); all P<.0001.
limits: Online sample, one probe trial per condition (binary switch). Authors reject arbitration by prediction errors and differential learning rates for T and R as alternatives. Strategy shifts across blocks not fully excluded.
agent_relevance: A policy change deep in a plan is as costly to a cached system as a structure change. A stored 'where this leads' memory must be invalidated when downstream rewards change which action is best, not only when transitions change.

source: Russek, Momennejad, Botvinick, Gershman, Daw (2017) Predictive representations can link model-based RL to model-free mechanisms
finding: Simulates Tolman-style tasks as grid worlds: latent learning, detour (transition change), reward devaluation, policy revaluation. SR-TD solves reward-change tasks and latent learning but fails detour, transition revaluation and policy revaluation, because it cannot update cached successors without new experience. Two fixes: dynamic recomputation of the SR, and SR-Dyna (replay of stored transitions to update the SR).
numbers: Qualitative simulations, medians across runs. Fig 6: with enough replay samples both SR-Dyna and Dyna-Q pass all three tasks. With too few samples Dyna-Q degrades to model-free and fails all three; SR-Dyna still passes latent learning but fails transition and policy revaluation.
limits: Small grid worlds. No new human data. 'Neurally plausible' is argued, not tested here.
agent_relevance: A ranked toolbox of compute cost versus flexibility: cache only, cache plus replay, full simulation. With a small compute budget a cached successor map degrades more gracefully than cached values.

source: Russek et al. (2017), cost of decision-time compute
finding: Argues that SR needs less decision-time computation than dynamic programming or tree search because the sum over future steps is done in advance. Cost moves from decision time to learning time and offline replay time.
numbers: Complexity argued in text; no timing benchmarks in the parts read.
limits: Trades compute for staleness.
agent_relevance: Pre-compute successor tables during idle or low-stakes steps and use them at decision time. In a scaffold: build 'what follows what' notes while exploring, not while answering.

source: Stachenfeld, Botvinick, Gershman (2017) The hippocampus as a predictive map
finding: Claims place cells encode rows or columns of the SR, not position. Predictions: place fields respect barriers; fields skew backward against direction of travel on a linear track; fields near a blocked path remap more than distant ones; grid cells reflect a low-dimensional eigendecomposition of the SR.
numbers: SR update: M(s,s') += alpha[I(s_t=s') + gamma M(s_{t+1},s') - M(s_t,s')], alpha=0.1 in simulations. Compared with Alvernhe et al. detour data (local remapping near barrier) and Hollup et al. annular watermaze data.
limits: Simulations matched to published experiments, qualitative. Mismatch noted by authors: Hollup found place fields the same size at reward, the SR predicts larger fields there ('still an incomplete account of reward-dependent place fields').
agent_relevance: The SR gives a principled map of a space of problems: close means 'leads to similar successors', not 'looks alike'. Useful for choosing which stored case to reuse.

source: Stachenfeld et al. (2017), grid cells and subgoals
finding: SR eigenvectors look like grid fields and shift with environment geometry as Krupic et al. found: aligned to boundaries in squares, more variable in circles, different across a trapezoid. SR eigenvectors equal graph Laplacian eigenvectors, so thresholding low-frequency ones gives bottleneck subgoals.
numbers: Reproduces qualitatively the multi-compartment grid data of Carpenter et al. (fields converge to a coherent grid over days; similarity between rooms falls near zero). Eigenvectors are invariant to the discount factor; eigenvalues change. Low-frequency smoothing acts as spectral regularisation.
limits: Simulation only. Many SR eigenvectors do not look like canonical grid cells.
agent_relevance: Bottleneck states found from successor structure are natural subgoals and checkpoints for a plan.

source: Kool, Cushman, Gershman (2016) When does model-based control pay off?
finding: In the original two-step task and common variants, model-based control did not raise reward rate, so the assumed accuracy versus effort trade-off is absent. Five task factors cause this. A redesigned task where planning pays raised model-based use.
numbers: Simulation: regression of weight w on reward rate near zero over all learning rates and inverse temperatures. Joint inclusion of the five factors raised the relationship about 230 times. Human test: 199 did the novel task, 381 analysed over both tasks. Median w 0.27 (Daw task) vs 0.48 (novel); rank-sum z=3.31, p<.001. w vs reward rate r=0.55 (novel, p<.001) vs r=0.10 (Daw, p=.15); group difference t(377)=4.71, p<.001.
limits: Online sample (Mechanical Turk). Supports a cost-benefit view; does not show the brain computes it.
agent_relevance: Check the expected win from planning: if simulation does not improve accuracy on a task class, do not pay for it. Per-class payoff gating of planning cost.

source: Akam, Costa, Dayan (2015) Simple plans or sophisticated habits? State, transition and learning interactions in the two-step task
finding: Shows by simulation that model-free strategies can masquerade as model-based in the two-step task. Task-structure changes create correlations between start-of-trial action values and later events, breaking trial-pair analyses. Model-free agents that use a latent state, or correlations between where reward is found and which action is good, look model-based even under more sophisticated analyses.
numbers: Simulations; a suggested analysis correction is confirmed to restore power for the first problem. No human data in the parts read.
limits: Read: abstract, author summary and discussion, not every simulation.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a stay/switch signature as proof of planning. For the agent: test whether a cached rule gives the same output before claiming 'I planned this' (G3 style).
quote: indicate the complexity of cleanly dissociating the contribution of different learning strategies to behaviour

source: Momennejad, Otto, Daw, Norman (2018) Offline replay supports planning in human reinforcement learning
finding: fMRI 2-step revaluation task. People replanned after reward changes. Multi-voxel evidence for off-task replay of the Stage I cue during rest predicted later replanning. Neural sensitivity to unsigned prediction error predicted replay.
numbers: N=24. Revaluation blocks: replanning t(23)=4.89, p<.0001; control t(23)=-0.10, p=.92; difference t(23)=4.333, p=.0002. Replay vs revaluation behaviour rho=0.54, p=.0068 (revaluation blocks), not in control blocks.
limits: Small sample, cluster threshold p<.005, correlational, replay decoded by a pattern classifier.
agent_relevance: Planning can be moved offline: replay past traces when surprise was high, then use the integrated result at decision time. Maps to a surprise-triggered consolidation pass in the agent, not a scheduled one.

source: Barreto, Dabney, Munos, Hunt, Schaul, van Hasselt, Silver (2017) Successor features for transfer in reinforcement learning
finding: Generalises the SR to successor features: if reward is a linear function of features, Q-values for any new reward weights are successor features dotted with the weights. With generalised policy improvement (take the best across stored policies), it transfers to a new task before any learning and gives a performance guarantee.
numbers: Two theorems on transfer bounds. Experiments: navigation sequence and a simulated 2-joint arm (12 target tasks), significantly outperforming Q-learning baselines (normalised return curves).
limits: Needs reward linear in known features and fixed dynamics. Results are curves, no single headline number read.
agent_relevance: Recipe: separate stored 'what the world does' from 'what this task wants'. A new goal reuses earlier experience by changing only a weight vector (a new rubric).

source: Sutton (1990) Integrated architectures for learning, planning and reacting based on approximating dynamic programming (Dyna)
finding: Dyna interleaves real experience with replayed simulated transitions from a learned model, so cached values improve between decisions. Basis for SR-Dyna. Not opened; described via Russek 2017.
numbers: none recorded
limits: Quality depends on enough replay samples (Russek Fig 6).
agent_relevance: Baseline for 'plan between actions, act from cache'.

source: Tolman (1948) Cognitive maps in rats and men
finding: Latent learning and shortcut/detour experiments, the founding evidence that animals form map-like knowledge beyond stimulus-response caching. Not opened.
numbers: none recorded
limits: Old behavioural work.
agent_relevance: Origin of the test: change the structure or reward and see if behaviour adjusts without new experience.

source: Gershman (2018) The successor representation: its computational logic and neural substrates
finding: Review of SR in behaviour and brain, including relation to MF/MB control and transfer. Not opened (fetch returned only a landing page).
numbers: none recorded
limits: Pointer only.
agent_relevance: Pointer for later reading.

source: Dayan (1993) and Russek (2017): policy dependence of the SR
finding: The SR stores visits under a specific policy. When reward changes the best action, the stored M is wrong for the new policy until relearned. Russek handles it with off-policy SR-Dyna and recomputation.
numbers: Policy revaluation failure shown in simulation (Fig 6C): SR-Dyna without enough replay passes latent learning but fails transition and policy revaluation.
limits: Successor features with generalised policy improvement (Barreto 2017) cover part of this.
agent_relevance: Store successor maps per policy or plan style, and mark which plan they were made under.

source: Momennejad (2017): why MF+MB hybrids cannot explain the asymmetry
finding: Formal argument: any weighted MF+MB mix scales the equal sensitivity of MB (equal on reward and transition) and cannot give an asymmetry. Only an SR component makes reward revaluation easier than transition revaluation.
numbers: Model comparison on group means: pure MB, pure SR and hybrid SR+MB (Fig 5). Hybrid fits best.
limits: Authors test and reject: different T and R learning rates; arbitration by state vs reward prediction errors. Forgetting is ruled out by the control condition.
agent_relevance: If an agent adapts equally to changes in value and in structure it is probably planning; a gap means a cache is in use. This is a measurable diagnostic of the agent's own memory type.

source: Kool et al. (2016): re-analysis of Daw, Dezfouli and Doll task versions
finding: In all three task versions the link between planning weight and reward rate is near zero. Doll's version shows more sensitivity at high inverse temperature and small learning rates, but participants' fits were not in that range.
numbers: Median weight w=0.27 in the Daw-task sample. Raw stay probability is not a clean measure of model-based influence (a different start state can raise stay after reward).
limits: Model-based weights were still nonzero, read as habit-like or effort-insensitive mixing.
agent_relevance: Mixed-control signatures are partly products of task payoff. Evaluate the agent's planner on tasks where planning pays off.

source: Kool et al. (2016): five factors that remove the planning payoff
finding: Five factors weaken the payoff of planning in the standard task. Each alone has a small effect (the original task is only about 1.3 SD from one-factor tasks), but together they multiply it.
numbers: Volume-under-surface metric over 32 tasks from 5 binary factors; joint effect about 230 times the original.
limits: Simulation with parameterised learners; humans tested on only two designs.
agent_relevance: When cache and planner usually agree, simulation is wasted. Gate planning on how often the two disagree.

source: Momennejad et al. (2018): surprise as replay trigger
finding: Unsigned prediction errors predict later replay and replanning. Prediction error and replay decline over blocks, consistent with replay targeting the surprising.
numbers: Rest 1 replay higher than Rest 2, t(23)=2.07, p=.049; another contrast t(23)=2.17, p=.039.
limits: Marginal p-values; N=24; correlational.
agent_relevance: Surprise as the trigger for deeper processing, the same logic as G1 (doubt only on a signal).

source: Stachenfeld et al. (2017): discount and horizon
finding: The discount factor sets how far ahead the map looks. Hippocampal place-field size grows along the longitudinal axis, read as a range of discounts. Locality of remapping after a barrier comes from the discount.
numbers: Eigenvectors independent of gamma; eigenvalues put more weight on large scales as gamma rises.
limits: Link between field-size gradient and gamma is an interpretation.
agent_relevance: Keep short-horizon and long-horizon summaries of what leads to what, not one.

source: Momennejad et al. (2017): individual differences and training caveats
finding: Individual differences were large with multi-modal revaluation scores. Training length varied by person.
numbers: Phase 1 ended after three correct preference reports or 20 stimuli. Time on task raised revaluation F(1,57.3)=9.92, P<.01, with no interaction by condition (F=0.15, P=.695).
limits: Authors: a pure SR does not explain the data; they claim only that some SR use exists.
agent_relevance: Treat 'SR in humans' as a partial component, and give the agent a fall-back to full simulation.

source: Dolan & Dayan (2013) Goals and habits in the brain
finding: Review of MF versus MB control, goals and habits, and disorders. Not opened.
numbers: none recorded
limits: Pointer only.
agent_relevance: Background for the MF/MB framing.

source: Sutton & Barto (2018) Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, 2nd ed.
finding: Textbook source for TD, Dyna and the model-free/model-based split. Not opened.
numbers: none recorded
limits: Pointer only.
agent_relevance: Reference definitions.
